---
title: "Defining regular languages"
bibliography: ../../formal_complexity.bib
---

The following definition can be found in @partee_mathematical_1990, Definition 17.10 (p. 465).

Given an alphabet Σ:

1. ∅ is a regular language.
2. For any string s ∈ Σ*, {s} is a regular language.
3. If A and B are regular languages, then so is A ∪ B.
4. If A and B are regular languages, then so is AB.
5. If A is a regular language, then so is A*.
6. Nothing else is a regular language, unless it being so follows from 1-5.

## Examples of regular languages

For all, Σ = {a, b, c}

1. Any finite language.

2. Strings in L consist of any number of as.

3. Strings in L consist of any number of as or bs.

4. Strings in L consist of any number of as, followed by any number of bs.

5. Strings in L begin with an a and end with a c.

6. Strings in L have ab as a substring.

7. Strings in L have exactly one a.

### Exercise

Show that each of the languages in 1--7 is regular, according to the definition of a regular language.
